what: The NIST curve-seeds audit — pre-registration, written 2026-10-16 (evening, Brazil) before any claim was decided at scale. A scout earlier the same evening had reproduced the nine NIST seeds from the man-page LCG in 40 lines (scratchpad; the red control ts+1 failed as it must) and nothing else; that scout is superseded by this record.
claimant: Anthropic, Frontier Red Team — "Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins", 2026-10-16 (corpus/curveseeds/sources/anthropic-ecdsa-curve-origins-2026-10-16.html, pinned). Authors as listed on the page. The post carries two Python blocks (CC0) that reproduce its numbers; they are pinned as evidence and NEVER executed here — every decision below is by code written from the POSIX specification of drand48, from ANSI X9.62's curve-derivation procedure as FIPS 186-2 prints its intermediates, and from FreeLIP's lip.c.

claims.S: SEEDS (14): each published 160-bit seed is the n-th 20-byte candidate of the lrand48 stream started by srand48(t) — prime curves: candidate n = lrand48 calls 20(n−1)+1 … 20n, each call contributing the byte lrand48() >> 23 (the top 8 bits of the 48-bit state); binary curves: srand48(t/2) with t/2 an integer division, candidate n = calls 5(n−1)+1 … 5n, each call contributing lrand48() as a 32-bit word. (t, n) per curve are the post's table (claim.table below). UTC. 1-based candidate index.
claims.D: DERIVATIONS (14): each seed yields the published curve under the SHA-1 procedure of ANSI X9.62-1998 — prime case: with t = bitlength(p), s = ⌊(t−1)/160⌋, v = t − 160s, c = (rightmost v bits of SHA-1(seed)) ‖ SHA-1(seed+1) ‖ … ‖ SHA-1(seed+s), and the published b satisfies b²·c ≡ −27 (mod p) (a = −3); FIPS 186-2 prints c for the five NIST prime curves and the certificate requires equality with it; the X9.62 example curves print no c, the congruence alone decides. Binary case: b (in the normal basis FIPS uses for s and b) = (rightmost v bits of SHA-1(seed)) ‖ SHA-1(seed+1) ‖ … with t = m. This claim is the standard's, not the post's; it is decided so that the chain timestamp → seed → published curve is closed by one record.
claims.G: BASE POINTS (6): for P-192 (= prime192v1), prime192v2, prime192v3, prime239v1, prime239v2, prime239v3 the published Gx is the first x on the curve produced by FreeLIP's generator — zrstarts(seed) with the LIP seed of the post's table; state ← state · 3^121 mod (2^107 − 1); zrandom(2^NBITS) = state mod 2^NBITS after the rejection step lip.c codes; seven zrandom draws discarded (the post's reading of the generating program); then zrandomb(p): ⌈bitlength(p)/NBITS⌉ + 1 limbs, the first drawn most significant, reduced mod p; repeat until x³ − 3x + b is a quadratic residue (Euler criterion = 1); NBITS = 26, FreeLIP's SINGLE_MUL build (lip.h). Gy is checked to square to x³ − 3x + b and which root it is recorded as a reading.
claims.R: READINGS, not decided here (listed on the page with what would decide them): R1 candidate 876 of the P-256 run, three P-224 candidates and seven X9.62 candidates also yield prime-order curves 'with parameters chosen the same way' — needs point counting at 192–256 bits (PARI's SEA, outside the standard library; an optional lane, counted apart if run); R2 the 1/5810 chance of the all-zero top bits — a null-model number; R3 'makes a backdoor much less plausible' — interpretation; R4 the binary curves' clock halved — the post's own hypothesis; R5 B-163's seed and the base points of P-224/256/384/521 and of the binary curves — open, and said so by the post; R6 the number of generation runs — unknowable from the numbers.

claim.source: the post's table (its first code block, read as data; its prose gives P-256's 1842 and the 'first 20 bytes are candidate 1' convention)

unexplained: P-224, P-256, P-384, P-521 base points
B-233, B-283, B-409, B-571 base points

published: corpus/curveseeds/published.json — read from the pinned FIPS 186-2 text layer and OpenSSL's ec_curve.c by tools/read-curveseeds-published.py; the two sources must agree on every NIST field or the reader refuses.

verdicts.CERTIFIED: the computation written here reproduces the published object bit for bit (a seed, c, the congruence, the normal-basis b, Gx)
verdicts.REFUTED: it does not, under the conventions stated in the claim; the record carries what was produced instead
verdicts.REFUSED: the decision needs a tool or a convention the record does not have (point counting; an ambiguous convention the post does not fix) — stated with the reason
verdicts.NEEDS DATA: an input the decision needs is published nowhere (the generating program; the number of runs)

arithmetic: integers only; Python's standard library (hashlib.sha1, int) in instruments/curveseeds/decide.py and, sharing no code, Node's BigInt with crypto's SHA-1 in instruments/curveseeds/decide.js; the two must agree on every field of every verdict or the run refuses.
calibration: before any claim is decided both deciders must (i) regenerate FIPS 186-2's printed c for P-256 from its printed seed, (ii) reproduce the POSIX example semantics (srand48(0) then lrand48 — no example value is normative, so the check is internal consistency: the state after srand48(t) has low 16 bits 330E), (iii) reproduce the FIPS-printed b of B-233 in the normal basis from its printed s.
redControls: the timestamp one second off must not reproduce the seed
the candidate index one off must not reproduce the seed
reading lrand48 as mrand48 (signed 32 bits) must not reproduce the seed
the binary clock not halved must not reproduce the seed
one seed byte flipped must break the derivation (c or the congruence)
SHA-1(seed − i) in place of SHA-1(seed + i) must not reproduce FIPS's c
a LIP seed one off must not reproduce Gx
NBITS = 30 in place of 26 must not reproduce Gx
a corrupted pin must refuse the run
the two deciders disagreeing on one field must refuse the run
whatCountsAsAResult: a verdict per claim row (14 S, 14 D, 6 G) with the object produced, the readings listed with what would decide each, and the optional point-counting lane's own counts if run. All CERTIFIED is a result and gets the same page.
notClaimed: that the timestamps are the moment the NSA ran its program (a 32-bit srand48 argument that reads as a 1997 date is the claim; the inference is the reader's); that no other generator produces the same bytes; anything about the security of the curves; anything about why candidates were skipped.
cost: laptop minutes for S, D, G; the optional lane hours of PARI on a laptop

amendments.date: 2026-10-16 (minutes after the pre-registration, before any claim row was decided)
amendments.after: the pre-registered calibration (i): regenerate FIPS 186-2's printed c for P-256 from its printed seed
amendments.seen: the first attempt produced c = fefba166… where FIPS prints 7efba166…; for P-192, b099d2bb against 3099d2bb — the leftmost bit of the first SHA-1 block is cleared. That is ANSI X9.62-1998 A.3.3.1's own rule for the prime case (set the leftmost bit of W0 to 0), omitted from the claims text above; the binary case A.3.3.2 has no such step and B-233's normal-basis b reproduced without it.
amendments.change: the prime derivation clears bit v−1 of the first block; a red control is added — the chain without the clearing must not reproduce c. Nothing else changes; the calibration against the standard's own printed intermediate is exactly what caught this.
amendments.notChanged: the claims, the verdicts, the pins, the red controls already listed
